lessons.title: What is different
lessons.objective: You can list the biggest rule differences between college and the NFL.

payload.prompt: Match each college rule difference to what it means.

pairs.definition: A college receiver needs only one foot inbounds to catch it, not two like in the NFL.
The clock keeps running after incompletions and out-of-bounds plays, speeding up college games.
Both teams start at the opponent's 25-yard line and get alternate possessions; from round three, teams must go for two.

explanation.summary: College uses a one-foot catch, a running clock and a shootout overtime. These rules create a faster, more explosive game.
explanation.sayThisLine: One foot, clock runs, shootout overtime. That is college ball.

payload.prompt: A receiver gets one foot down and catches the ball before stepping out. That is a catch in college. True or false?

scene.alt: A receiver making a one-foot catch against the sideline in college.

explanation.correct: True. College only needs one foot. The NFL requires two feet or another body part in bounds.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, one foot is enough in college. That is the biggest receiver rule difference.

payload.prompt: What happens to the college clock when a receiver goes out of bounds on an incomplete pass?

options.text: The clock stops until the next snap
The clock keeps running until the next play starts
The clock stops for two seconds then resumes

explanation.correct: The clock keeps running. That is the college rule: fewer stops, faster game, and teams manage time differently than in the NFL.
explanation.incorrect: In college, the clock runs after incompletions and out-of-bounds plays. Only certain plays stop it: timeouts, the end of quarters, and a few penalties.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: They took it to overtime. From the third overtime on, both teams have to go for two. That completely changes the strategy.

payload.question: What is the analyst saying?

options.text: Overtime lasts three rounds no matter what
After two full rounds of overtime, teams must go for two instead of kicking, making it riskier and faster
Teams can score safeties in overtime
Overtime only happens once per game

payload.translation: College overtime is a shootout. Start at the 25, alternate possessions, kick the first two tries, but from round three every touchdown requires a two-point attempt. It is sudden-death strategy.

followUps.line: Why would a team go for two on the third round instead of kicking?
followUps.why: Tests understanding: if both teams go for two, a failed kick and a failed two-point try both end the game, but two-point tries are riskier and higher-reward.

followUps.line: Is this the same as NFL overtime?
followUps.why: No. The NFL has regular sudden-death with a twist: both teams get a possession in the regular season. College is a completely different system.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about why the analyst emphasized the third overtime. It is because the mandatory two-point rule kicks in.

payload.prompt: Tied in overtime, third round. Your team scores a touchdown. Kick or go for two?

situation.narrative: Third round of college overtime, both teams tied.

facts.label: Rule
facts.value: Must go for two from the 3-yard line

options.label: Go for two
options.consequence: You must go for two by rule. Your two-point play is your best bet to win. If you fail, the other team has a chance to also score and continue.
considerations: The rule mandates two-point tries from round three.

options.label: Kick the extra point
options.consequence: You cannot. College overtime rules require a two-point attempt from the third round onward.
considerations: Knowing the rule is essential to understanding college football's intensity.

payload.expertNote: College overtime forces aggression from round three. It is why college overtime games are so wild and unpredictable.

lessons.title: Polls and the committee
lessons.objective: You can explain how college rankings and the playoff committee decide the top teams.

payload.prompt: Which poll matters most for getting into the College Football Playoff?

options.text: The AP poll, which has been around since 1936
The Coaches poll, which is coaches voting on quality
The CFP committee rankings, which are kept secret until late season

explanation.correct: The CFP committee is what matters. Their rankings in November and December decide who gets in. AP and Coaches polls are historical but less official now.
explanation.incorrect: The committee rankings are what actually decide the 12-team field. They start revealing rankings in November and update weekly.

payload.prompt: Put the CFP selection order in the right sequence.

items.text: Four conference champions and the highest-ranked non-champion from a Power Five get automatic bids
The remaining eight spots go to the best-ranked teams from any conference
The top four seeds get byes in the first round; five through twelve play in the first round
The four winners advance to the semifinals to determine the national champion

explanation.correct: The 12-team format guarantees conference champions a shot but fills the rest by ranking. Seeds one through four rest.
explanation.incorrect: The playoff seeding prioritizes automatic bids for power conferences, then fills remaining spots by ranking.

payload.prompt: Match each ranking system to its role.

pairs.definition: Media voter rankings; affects perception but does not seed the playoff.
Rankings by head coaches; historic but less official now.
Official ranker for playoff selection; their Tuesday rankings matter most.

explanation.summary: Three ranking systems exist: media votes, coach votes, and the official committee. Only the committee decides the playoff.
explanation.sayThisLine: AP is media. Coaches is coaches. CFP committee is the one that matters.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: We dropped to number five but the committee has us at two. The media does not respect us at all.

payload.question: What is the fan saying?

options.text: The AP poll and CFP committee always agree
The committee might rank them higher than the media does, which matters more for the playoff
The media polls determine who gets into the playoff
Rankings never change after November

payload.translation: The fan is relieved that the official committee (CFP) ranks their team higher than the AP poll. The committee is what matters for playoff seeding, not media opinion.

followUps.line: Why would the committee rank a team higher than the media?
followUps.why: Tests understanding: the committee watches games and has specific criteria; the media polls are a popularity contest.

followUps.line: Does a team get in on AP poll ranking or committee ranking?
followUps.why: Committee. Only the CFP committee rankings matter for playoff selection.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, remember that the committee is the official selector; media rankings are influential but not binding.

payload.prompt: Every Power Five conference champion gets an automatic bid to the CFP. True or false?

scene.alt: A conference champion's celebration after earning a CFP bid.

explanation.correct: True. Every Power Five conference champion gets in. Plus the best non-champion Group of Five champion. That is six auto bids guaranteed.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, auto bids to all Power Five champs is a core rule. It is why winning your conference matters so much.

lessons.title: The 12-team playoff
lessons.objective: You can explain how the playoff bracket works, who gets byes and what a first-round win means.

payload.prompt: Put the playoff rounds in order.

items.text: First round: Seeds five through twelve play; seeds one through four get byes and play the winners
Quarterfinals: Eight teams (the bye teams plus four first-round winners) play in four games
Semifinals: The four winners play in two games, often in bowl stadiums
National championship: The two survivors play for the title

explanation.correct: Twelve teams, four bye to the quarterfinals, eight play first, then down to four, then two, then one champion.
explanation.incorrect: The playoff format proceeds from first round through quarterfinals, semifinals, and then the national championship.

payload.prompt: Why is a number-one seed so valuable in the college playoff?

options.text: They play fewer games in the early rounds because they get a bye to the quarterfinals
They always face a weaker team in the semifinals
They get home games in the first round

explanation.correct: The number-one seed rests while seeds five through twelve play. That rest and the bye are huge advantages.
explanation.incorrect: The bye is the advantage. Seeds one through four get a first-round rest; seeds five through twelve play immediately.

payload.prompt: You are a fan of the number-eight seed. You barely made the field. What are your chances?

facts.label: If you win
facts.value: Face number one or four seed in the quarterfinals

facts.label: Rest disadvantage
facts.value: The one seed has had two weeks off

options.label: Acknowledge it is an uphill climb
options.consequence: Your team is in because of ranking, not a bye. You face the five seed immediately and, if you win, jump to a rested top-four team. That is the eight-seed story.
considerations: Cinderella runs happen but it is a tough path.

options.label: Think you are guaranteed to advance
options.consequence: The five seed is strong, and every match-up in the first round is competitive. Nothing is guaranteed.
considerations: Making the playoff is hard. Winning from eight is harder.

payload.expertNote: Being an eight seed is both an honor and a huge disadvantage. You have to play to survive; the top four get to rest.

payload.prompt: Match each playoff round to what it is called and who plays.

pairs.definition: Seeds five through twelve play in four games at campus sites; the bye teams (one through four) rest.
The four bye teams play the four first-round winners in four games, often at major bowl stadiums.
The four quarterfinal winners play in two games in bowl venues. Tradition: the Orange Bowl and Cotton Bowl (or others).

explanation.summary: First round is for seeds five-twelve at home fields. Quarterfinals bring the bye teams in. Semifinals are bowls with the final four.
explanation.sayThisLine: Five through twelve first, then bye teams play them, then go to bowls.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: We have to finish in the top four or we are playing an extra game. Every team playing eight games in the playoffs instead of seven is a huge difference.

payload.question: What is the coach saying?

options.text: All twelve teams play the same number of games
Getting a bye and resting is a major advantage in the playoffs
Winning a first-round game guarantees a bye
The playoff is best of seven games

payload.translation: The coach is emphasizing that the bye (seeds one through four not playing the first round) is a strategic advantage. His team plays seven games if it gets a bye but eight if it plays first round.

followUps.line: How does rest affect playoff performance?
followUps.why: Tests understanding: extra rest means fresher players, more time to prepare, and mental recovery from the regular season.

followUps.line: Is the bye worth giving up a higher seed?
followUps.why: Maybe not. A two seed with a bye is good, but a four seed with a bye is marginal. Context matters.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about the value of a week off in sports. Every team wants extra rest.

lessons.title: Conference chaos
lessons.objective: You can explain why colleges move conferences and what realignment means to rivalries.

payload.prompt: Why do colleges leave conferences?

options.text: More television money, better playoff odds, and wanting to join stronger leagues
The coaching staff asked for it
The current conference was too old

explanation.correct: Money and prestige drive realignment. The SEC and Big Ten offer bigger TV deals and better playoff seeding. Schools chase that.
explanation.incorrect: Realignment is economics: TV deals, playoff positioning, and brand. It is not about nostalgia or tradition.

statement.speaker: Longtime Fan
statement.text: Our rival just moved to the Big Ten. We might never play them again. This realignment stuff is destroying college football.

payload.question: What is the fan saying?

options.text: Conference realignment has ended century-old rivalries because schools left for money
The Big Ten is a bad conference
Rivalries will definitely never happen again
Schools should not be allowed to move

payload.translation: The fan is upset that his school's traditional rival left for another conference, likely ending the annual game that had been played for decades. Realignment has broken many historic rivalries.

followUps.why: Sometimes, but out-of-conference games are harder to schedule. The tradition matters less than TV money now.

followUps.line: Is this good or bad for college football?
followUps.why: Opinion. Fans miss traditions; schools get more money and better playoff access. Both are true.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about what realignment means: schools splitting apart, traditional rivals separated, new conferences formed.

payload.prompt: Match each realignment effect to what it means.

pairs.definition: Rivals move conferences and no longer play. Fans lose traditions.
Better TV deals give schools more money for athletics.
Strong conferences improve playoff odds and prestige.

explanation.summary: Realignment chases money and power. Rivalries suffer; revenue grows; strong conferences get stronger.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rivalries die, money rises, power consolidates. That is realignment.

payload.prompt: Tradition and history are the main reasons schools stay in conferences. True or false?

scene.alt: A historic rivalry matchup with crowds and tradition.

explanation.correct: False. Money is the main driver. Schools leave historic conferences for bigger TV deals and better playoff positioning.
explanation.incorrect: Tradition matters to fans, but not to university boards. Money and competitive access drive realignment.

payload.prompt: Your school is offered a $30M annual raise to join a new conference. You lose your 80-year rivalry. Worth it?

facts.label: Stakeholders
facts.value: Players, coaches, and fans all have opinions

options.label: Take the money and join
options.consequence: Schools make this choice almost every time. Money funds scholarships, facilities and programs. Rivalries are emotions; budgets are real.
considerations: $30M is enormous. It affects player compensation, facilities, and program quality.

options.label: Keep the rivalry and tradition
options.consequence: Few schools choose this. Tradition matters to fans, not enough to turn down tens of millions of dollars.
considerations: In the current climate, this is a losing strategy.

payload.expertNote: Realignment is about money, not history. Schools overwhelmingly choose revenue over tradition when forced to choose.

lessons.title: Portal and NIL
lessons.objective: You can explain why college rosters turn over completely every year.

payload.prompt: You are a college quarterback benched after three games. The transfer portal opens in a week. Stay or leave?

facts.label: Current team
facts.value: Might get you back in eventually

options.label: Enter the portal
options.consequence: Most players do this now. No sit-out rule means you can play immediately for a new team. One bench game ends your season if you wait.
considerations: The portal gives players power. Coaches lost leverage.

options.label: Stay and compete
options.consequence: Possible, but risky. You are behind on the depth chart and might not get a chance. Few choose to wait anymore.
considerations: Patience is rare when immediate playing time is available elsewhere.

payload.expertNote: The transfer portal changed college football completely. Players are free agents after the season ends. Rosters turn over overnight.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: Half my roster is new guys from the portal. We have to rebuild team chemistry every single year now.

payload.question: What is the coach saying?

options.text: The transfer portal makes it easy to draft college players now
College rosters change drastically every year because players transfer freely, and team chemistry suffers
The coach is not doing a good job recruiting
College players stay with their teams for four years like they used to

payload.translation: The coach is frustrated that half his team is new portal transfers. Building chemistry and a stable roster is harder now that players can leave anytime.

followUps.line: Why would a top recruit leave after signing?
followUps.why: Tests understanding: better offer elsewhere, portal opportunity, promise broken, or lack of playing time.

followUps.line: Is the transfer portal good or bad for college football?
followUps.why: Opinion. Players like the freedom; coaches hate the instability; fans miss roster continuity.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think: in the old days, players stayed four years. Now they leave after one bad season. That is the portal.

payload.prompt: Match each new money system to what it does.

pairs.definition: Lets players transfer freely with no sit-out. They play immediately.
Players earn from endorsements and sponsors, not just scholarships.
Colleges share athletic revenue directly with athletes since 2025.

explanation.summary: Portal lets players move. NIL lets them earn from their name. Revenue sharing gives them a cut of the pie. Together they transform college recruiting.
explanation.sayThisLine: Free to move, paid for your name, given a share of the money. That is modern college ball.

payload.prompt: A college player can transfer and play immediately for a new team without sitting out. True or false?

scene.alt: A transfer player joining a new team and stepping onto the field.

explanation.correct: True. The portal allows immediate eligibility. No sit-out penalty. That is why transfers happen so quickly.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, players can transfer and be eligible right away. The sit-out rule is gone.

payload.prompt: Which change has most disrupted college football recruiting?

options.text: The transfer portal and NIL letting players leave and earn money from their name immediately
Coaches being paid less money
The NFL draft happening earlier in the year

explanation.correct: Portal + NIL is the earthquake. Players can leave at any time, earn from their name, and play immediately. That is unprecedented freedom.
explanation.incorrect: The portal and NIL are the dual disruptions. Together they gave players power they never had before.

lessons.title: Recruiting
lessons.objective: You can decode recruiting talk and understand why college recruiting never stops.

payload.prompt: Match each recruiting term to what it means.

pairs.definition: Highest-ranked high school player; expected NFL star.
All prospects signed by a team that year, ranked together.
When high school seniors sign with college teams.

explanation.summary: Recruiting is about landing high school talent. Stars are rated on a scale; classes are ranked as a group; signing day is the spectacle.
explanation.sayThisLine: Five stars are elite, classes are groups, signing day is the show.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Our recruiting class is ranked number twelve nationally. Half of them will probably transfer out by spring.

payload.question: What is the fan saying?

options.text: The recruiting class is elite and no one will leave
A top-twelve class is good but many recruits might leave via the portal if they do not play or fit the system
Recruiting class rankings never matter
No one leaves college once they sign

payload.translation: The fan is being realistic. Even highly recruited players transfer quickly if they are unhappy, benched or want to play immediately. A good ranking does not guarantee retention.

followUps.line: Why would a top recruit leave after signing?
followUps.why: Tests understanding: better offer elsewhere, portal opportunity, promise broken, or lack of playing time.

followUps.line: Is recruiting still important if everyone transfers?
followUps.why: Yes, but less. Strong recruiting is necessary but no longer sufficient to win.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think: a five-star has options. If unhappy, he uses the portal to leave.

payload.prompt: A team with five-star recruits will definitely win more games than a team with three-star recruits. True or false?

scene.alt: A high school star being recruited by multiple colleges.

explanation.correct: False. Star ratings are predictions, not guarantees. Coaching, development and fit matter. Many five-stars do not pan out; some lower-stars overachieve.
explanation.incorrect: Recruiting rankings are useful but imperfect. A three-star program with great coaching can beat a five-star program with poor development.

payload.prompt: How has the transfer portal changed recruiting?

options.text: Recruiting high school talent is now only half the battle; portal recruiting for transfers is equally important
Recruiting high school players is more important than ever
Recruiting does not happen anymore

explanation.correct: Strong programs now do both: recruit high school stars and poach portal players from other teams. Transfers fill gaps and provide immediate contributors.
explanation.incorrect: High school recruiting matters but so does the portal now. Top programs win the portal wars as much as the high school game.

payload.prompt: You are a five-star quarterback. Multiple schools want you. What matters most?

facts.label: Your choice
facts.value: Elite A or rising school B

facts.label: School A
facts.value: Storied, huge facilities, benched behind senior

options.label: Go to School B for immediate playing time
options.consequence: Five-stars choose playing time and NIL money now. A national title at School B or a backup role at School A? Players choose B.
considerations: Playing time is currency in modern recruiting.

options.label: Go to School A for the prestigious name
options.consequence: Some still do this. School A's brand and NFL pipeline are valuable. But you risk a bench year and portal transfer later.
considerations: Prestige matters, but not enough if you do not play.

payload.expertNote: Modern recruiting is about playing time, portal flexibility, and NIL money. The storied names still matter but not as much as before.

lessons.title: Heisman and awards
lessons.objective: You can say what a Heisman campaign is and why it matters to recruiting and draft stock.

payload.prompt: What is the Heisman Trophy?

options.text: The annual award for the most outstanding player in college football, voted on by fans and media
The trophy given to the national champion
An award only for running backs

explanation.correct: The Heisman is the individual player award, not a team award. It goes to the best player that year, any position.
explanation.incorrect: Heisman is the Oscars of college football. One player, any position, voted by voters in December.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: His Heisman campaign is in full swing. Every media story, every highlight reel, every stat is designed to remind voters he belongs.

payload.question: What is the analyst describing?

options.text: The player is running for political office
The orchestrated effort to get a player's name in front of voters for the Heisman award
The player is injured and cannot play
The team is losing games

payload.translation: A Heisman campaign is the strategic push to get a player in the award conversation. Teams, media, and even players push stats and highlights to voters all season.

followUps.why: Tests understanding: fans, coaches, media, and former players. It is a huge voter base.

followUps.line: Can a player on a bad team win a Heisman?
followUps.why: Rarely. The award usually goes to a star on a winning team. Individual excellence matters but team context helps a lot.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about the Oscars: campaigning, highlighting performances, and voting. The Heisman is very similar.

payload.prompt: Match each college football award to what it honors.

pairs.definition: Most outstanding player in college football.
Title for the CFP playoff winner.
Elite players at each position; stepping stone to NFL.

explanation.summary: Heisman is one player. National title is the team. All-America is the all-star team. Each matters for different reasons.
explanation.sayThisLine: Heisman is the best player. Championship is the best team. All-America is the elite squad.

payload.prompt: Winning a Heisman almost always means a player will be drafted high in the NFL draft. True or false?

scene.alt: A Heisman winner being drafted by an NFL team.

explanation.correct: True. Heisman winners are consistently top-ten NFL draft picks. The award is a strong indicator of NFL readiness.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, the Heisman comes with huge draft stock. It is the college football credential for the next level.

payload.prompt: You are a star running back on a five-loss team. Can you win a Heisman?

facts.label: Heisman voters
facts.value: Often favor players on winning teams

options.label: Very unlikely
options.consequence: Heisman almost always goes to a star on a winning team. Your elite stats are hurt by your team's record and playoff irrelevance.
considerations: Individual excellence on a bad team rarely wins the award.

options.label: You are a lock
options.consequence: Not true. Voters factor in team success and national relevance. Your 5-7 team is a drag on your resume.
considerations: Context matters hugely for the Heisman.

payload.expertNote: Heisman voters reward individuals on winning teams. A star on a losing team does not get the award, no matter how great the stats.

lessons.title: Rivalry week
lessons.objective: You can talk about rivalry games without insulting anyone and understand why they matter.

statement.speaker: Longtime Fan
statement.text: In a rivalry game, records do not matter. Everything we learned during the season gets thrown out. It is pure passion and tradition.

payload.question: What is the fan saying?

options.text: Rivalry games are just normal games with a lot of emotion
Rivalry games transcend records and stats; tradition and pride override normal game logic
Rivalry games are played in a different season
Rivalries have no impact on the playoff picture

payload.translation: The fan means that in a rivalry, a 3-9 team can beat a 12-0 team because the matchup and history override everything else. Rivalry games are unpredictable because passion trumps skill.

followUps.line: Do rivalry games follow predictable patterns?
followUps.why: No. Upsets are common. A bad team plays like a dynasty when pride and tradition are on the line.

followUps.line: Why do rivalries matter if they are just regular games?
followUps.why: They are not just games. They are cultural events. Losing a rivalry stings for a year.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about why fans care so much about rivalry games beyond just winning or losing.

payload.prompt: Match each rivalry element to what it represents.

pairs.definition: Game played for decades; Ohio State-Michigan (1897).
Annual match where records don't matter; pride does.
Pre-game party where both fans gather. Part of tradition.

explanation.summary: Rivalries are traditions first, games second. Every rivalry has a history, a yearly matchup, and a unique culture.
explanation.sayThisLine: History is the tradition, the game is the event, the tailgate is the culture.

payload.title: Talking about a big rivalry game
payload.setting: During rivalry week, when emotions are high.

exchanges.theirMessage: I cannot wait for the rivalry game next week. We always lose to them, but this year feels different.

replies.text: Why does this year feel different? What have you seen that makes you optimistic?
replies.theirResponse: Our quarterback has been amazing this season and their defense is banged up.
replies.coachNote: Shows you care about her reasoning, not just her emotion.

replies.theirResponse: They are. I hope we finally beat them.
replies.coachNote: True, but vague. Dig into her specific prediction.

replies.text: You always say that and you always lose.
replies.coachNote: Do not laugh at her optimism. She is sharing her hope.

payload.prompt: What happens to a team after losing a big rivalry game?

options.text: The loss stings more than a regular loss and fans stay upset for weeks
It is the same as any other loss
The team is eliminated from the playoffs

explanation.correct: Rivalry losses hurt differently. Fans are frustrated for weeks, recruiting is affected, and the team dreams of next year's revenge.
explanation.incorrect: Rivalry losses are not just losses. They carry cultural weight that lasts until next season's matchup.

payload.prompt: Your team is 3-9 and the rival is 9-3, heading into their matchup. What is the likely outcome?

facts.label: Stakes
facts.value: Bragging rights and rival team's playoff fate

options.label: Your team has a real shot to upset them
options.consequence: In a rivalry, a 3-9 team can absolutely beat a 9-3 team. Pride, tradition and no pressure are powerful. Upsets happen constantly in rivalries.
considerations: The better team does not always win in rivalries.

options.label: The 9-3 team is guaranteed to win
options.consequence: No guarantee in a rivalry. Your team might be motivated precisely because they have nothing to lose.

payload.expertNote: Rivalry upsets are famous because they happen so often. A bad team can absolutely upset a good rival when tradition and pride matter.
